Missing at Sea

By: Annalise Lubbe | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
When a deep sea fishing trawler sank off the coast of Cape Town, only 9 men survived, 11 went missing. Now their families are asking what happened and why.

Unique Selling Point:
On Friday 17 May the unexplainable and most unexpected happened: The Lepanto, a deep sea fishing trawler, disappeared in a matter of minutes off the coast of Table Bay. Two life rafts were on board. Nine men clung onto the one, the second blew away in the wind. Eleven men could not be saved and disappeared into the ocean.

Summary:
On Thursday 16 May the MFV Lepanto deep sea fishing trawler were brought back due to some enjin problems. Later that day, the Lepanto carrying 20 crew members went back out to sea to continue their fishing. They were trawling hake 34 nautical miles west off Slangkop light.

On Friday 17 May at 15h30 a distress call came from the MFV Armana, a vessel trawling fish near the Lepanto. The Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre picked up the Mayday call from the Armanis that the Lepanto was in trouble and sinking rapidly. Within 3 minutes the vessel vanished. The only sign of life were 9 crew hanging onto a life raft desperate to get to the Armanis as they contend with meter swells and rough seas. They were not wearing any life jackets but with the assistance of the men on the Armanis they were brought safely onto the vessel.

The NSRI were called in to assist and sent a rescue craft to the site where the Lepanto disappeared. They had to race to the site which was 35 nautical miles away and took an hour. Three more vessels joined the search but there was no sign of life, life jackets or the usual signs like oil spills and debris. The search and rescue continued on Saturday but even with the help of a fixed wing aircraft to scan the ocean, they could not find any signs of life, only a few pieces of debris floating in the area where the Lepanto disappeared. The depth of the ocean was measured at 300 meters, too deep to send divers down to look for the bodies. It is presumed that the Lepanto turned upside down, trapping the men underneath.

On Sunday, barely three days later, the search was called off. The decision was made by The Maritime Rescue Operation Centre. Sea Harvest employer, CEO Felix Rhateb stated: “in view of the significant time elapsed since the accident we are calling off the search. Tragically, the men are now presumed drowned.”

It is reportedly one of the worst maritime fishing accidents in the history of Sea Harvest, said Rhateb when he met with the families. Also present at a gathering on Tuesday with the families were the mayor of Cape Town, the premier, and the minister of DEFF to give condolences.

At a special service held for the families on Thursday at the Cruise Terminal in Cape Town both survivors and family members spoke out. Benjamin van Wyk lost his son Jeremiah. He was asking where the bodies are? Why did they not go down looking for the men? And how can he find peace if there is no corpse to bury.

A moment of silence was given for the missing men presumed drowned. One by one the names of the eleven men were called out.

In the Isaacs home near Chatsworth on the West Coast, there is so much grief among the sisters and the mother. They lost their 26 year old brother, Johnwill, nicknamed “Jangle”. They too have questions about the accident and what could have happened why they have lost the center of the family so early in his life.


Further information:
A tragedy of this magnitude runs deep in the circles of seafaring men when they rely on each other through storms and difficulties. One of the survivors we spoke to, Nomrico Prins, said he is haunted by the cries he heard of the men trapped inside the vessel before it went down. The families who lost sons and husbands are blaming Sea Harvest for giving up and not spending money to find the bodies at the bottom of the sea and bringing them back to shore to be buried.

An investigation has been launched by the South African Maritime Safety Authority (SAMSA) into the history of the vessel, the repairs conducted and the service record amongst others. The investigation is ongoing and we will not be able to interview SAMSA at this stage.

The story:
It will be a personal account of what the families went through: from the moment they received news of the accident to what transpired since then and what the future holds. Their special memories of the men they lost and what they most remember of their loved ones. For them the future is uncertain. They have not been told how long the investigation will take to establish the cause of the accident; if they will ever find the bodies and when they will find peace of mind to bury their loved ones. We will also get a first hand account from one of the survivors, Nomrico Prins, who told us they experienced engine problems on the Lepanto and had to return to port after only two days at sea. He will also share his story of what happened during those last hours and minutes before Lepanto disappeared.

The company Sea Harvest declined to be interviewed at the last moment as they said an investigation by the South African Maritime Safety Authority (SAMSA) into the incident is still underway. In a Right of Reply they confirmed that Sea Harvest vessels are governed by a comprehensive maintenance system, with adherence to a robust and ongoing mandatory service regime as described by the authorities. They also said their efforts are focussed on ensuring the families of the missing crew are supported during this challenging time.

We will ‘revisit’ the rescue mission going back hours and days when it happened through the story of one of the survivors, Nomrico Prins.

For the bereaved families it is particularly difficult as they are waiting for the investigation to be concluded to find out why the accident happened. They are also waiting to hear when the men will officially be declared dead in order to bury their loved ones.

Interviews: Two families who have lost a loved one: The Isaac family who lost Johnwill Isaacs, and Benjamin van Wyk who lost his son, Jeremiah. We will also hear from Cleeve Robertson, CEO NSRI what the search and rescue operation for the Lepanto crew entailed.

Script:


Script: Lost at Sea
Duration: 12 minutes

Up sound: Mayday mayday…
V/O1 It’s exactly 26 minutes to four in the afternoon on Friday the 17th of May this year. A deep-sea vessel called MFV Armana issues a Mayday call. Another boat, the MFV Lepanto, is sinking off the Cape coast.
Nomrico Prins: Op die een oomblik was ek nog op die skip (One moment I was on the vessel,) en die ander oomblik toe le ek in die water en spartel vir my lewe. (and the next moment I was fighting for my life.) Als het so gou gebeur. (Everything happened so quickly.)
V/O2 Nomrico Prins is one of 20 crew on board the Lepanto, a fishing trawler owned by the company, Sea Harvest. He’s one of just nine survivors who jumped overboard and clung to a life raft.
Nomrico Prins: Daar was nie eens kans om lifejackets nie, (There wasn’t even a chance to put on lifejackets…) als was so gou, seker 5 minute. (everything happened so quickly…) Toe’s als oor. (Five minutes, then it was all over.)
V/O3 The remaining eleven crew, trapped inside the vessel, are heard crying for help as it disappears below the surface.
V/O4: Now the subject of an investigation, the Lepanto tragedy has left nearly a dozen families grieving for loved ones lost at sea; their hopes for closure frustrated by uncertainty over whether their bodies will ever be retrieved.
Pause music up
LINK: Crews on deep sea trawlers spend days, weeks at sea, braving the elements. It's a hard job risking life and limb and safe return is never guaranteed.
V/O5 Nomrico worked for Sea Harvest as a deckhand on the Lepanto for eleven years, forming a deep connection with his fellow crew.
Nomrico Prins: Ek kan dit nie beskryf nie maar ons was soos n familie, elke dag saam. (I can’t describe it, but like a family, we were together every day.) Met elke trip is die 20 saam mekaar. (We were together every day…on every trip us 20 men were together)
V/O6 Johnwill Isaacs left his home on the West Coast and signed up for the fishing life at just 17.
Lena Isaacs: Johnwill’s mother - En hy het vir my gese hy wil nou beginne werk, hy wil nou see toe gaan. (Then he told me he wants to work - he wants to work at sea) Toe het ek altyd teen die skare geskop en vir hom gese my hart is nie vir jou om op die see te werk nie (I kicked against the idea and said to him, “My heart doesn’t want you to go to sea”.) Maar ek het vir die Here gevra en die Here het my kalmte gegee dat hy maar gegaan het.(But then I asked the Lord, and He brought me peace - so I let my son go.)
V/O7 Johnwill, who had a close relationship with his two sisters, worked as deckhand on the Lepanto for 5 years.
Marisha Isaacs: Johnwill’s sister - As hy so van die see afgekom het (When he returned from the sea,) sal hy altyd unexpected opdaag by my, net om te kom hello se. (he would drop by unexpectedly, just to say hello,)
Chrizelda Bock: Johnwill’s sister: Hy was baie lief vir diere.(He was fond of animals.) Vriendelike man. (A friendly man.)
V/O8 The last time Johnwill’s family saw him alive was when he left for Cape Town’s harbour on the Tuesday before the tragedy.
Fade to black
V/9 The Lepanto left Cape Town port at 10 to 10 on 14th of May with 20 crew on board including Johnwill and Nomrico. According to Nomrico the vessel soon experienced engine trouble and had to return to port barely 24 hours later.
Nomrico Prins: Daar n problem op die main enjin soos hulle gese het (They said there was a problem with the main engine…) Dit was die fuel timing van die skip.(the fuel timing of the vessel was out.)
Up sound
V/O10 This video is taken from the deck of the Lepanto while it was being maintained in Cape Town harbour.
V/O11 After 14 hours on the slipway, the Lepanto returned to sea at 8 minutes past 4 on that Thursday afternoon.
Nomrico Prins: Ons het die donderdag aand, daai is omtrent nege uur (On the Thursday night, ‘round about nine o’clock,) wat die kaptein vir ons gese het ons gaan nou weer skiet (the captain said we are going to shoot again) om te kyk of als reg is (to see if everything is alright -)of die enjin die krag het om te tou.(if the engine still has power to hoist.)
V/O12 Shooting refers to sending the fishing gear to the seabed.
Pause
V/O13 At 2pm on Friday the 17th of May, the captain ordered that the trawl doors be shut. Minutes later disaster struck.
Nomrico Prins: Ons, ek was seker nog nie af by die trappies om te kom by die port side (I barely reached the bottom of the steps) en toe sien ek net hier gaan le die skip (when I saw the ship tilting…) en ek se vir myself “kom nou kom nou kom nou” (I said to myself, “Come now, come now!”) ek se nog vir myself “kom nou kom nou” (I said to myself, “Come now, come now!”) en ek het net gevoel een gryp my van agter af en hy ruk my toe op. (Then I felt someone grab me from behind and he pulled me up.) En hy se Rico die skip gaat val (And he said, “Rico the vessel is going to fall!”) en toe het hy al klaar gesien die mast touch die water (And then he already saw the mast falling into the water,) en ‘doef’ toe le die skip op sy een kant. (and ‘“dooof”! The ship was lying on its side.)
V/O14 Nomrico’s recollection of those last, chaotic minutes is sketchy. He was overcome with shock but he says he heard nothing out of the ordinary in the minutes before the ship went down. At least one of the crew could not swim
Nomrico Prins: En hy het net gese ouens is alright ek kan nie swem nie (And he said, “No, guys. It’s alright. I can’t swim.) en toe gaan hy af die eerste keer (Then he lifted his hands like this and went down the first time.) Toe kom hy weer op. (Then he came up again, then went straight down.) Toe gat hy net straight af en ons het hom nooit weer gesien nie.(We never saw him after that.)
LONG PAUSE here
Nomrico Prins: Want ek kon net gehoor het hoe daai drie keer geskree het (All I could hear were the screams.) Here mammie, help Here. En toe is dit als doodstil.(God, mommy, help God”,) Toe’s als doodstil. (and then it was dead quiet.) Toe is daar niks meer geskreery nie.(There was no more crying.)
LONG PAUSE
V/O15 One would think being able to swim is key to surviving an accident at sea. But the internationally recognised certifications standard required by all seafarers working on commercial vessels only teaches basic survival techniques, not how to swim.

Pause
V/O16 The nine survivors were rescued by the Armana, the vessel that had issued the original Mayday.
UP cellphone video clip of the rescue
V/O17 Four other vessels responded to a mayday broadcast by the Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre, and the National Sea Rescue Institute was alerted.
LINK: One of the NSRI rescue craft left from this space at Hout Bay harbour and headed to the Lepanto’s last known location, 35 nautical miles from the coast.
Dr Cleeve Robertson - CEO National Sea Rescue Institute: When the crew got on scene, understanding they arrived fairly close to last light and then searched into the night.
V/O18 Dr Cleeve Robertsona heads up the NSRI, staffed by dedicated volunteers.
Dr Cleeve Robertson: To assist them search at night they used illumination flares, very much like a distress signal in the darkness of night, it is very difficult.
V/O19 The NRSI saves hundreds of fishers in distress every year. On this mission their crew battled the darkness, howling 40 knot winds and 4 to 6 meter swells.
Pause
V/O20 Most of the next of kin were notified of the incident that same evening. Marisha says her family never received a call from Sea Harvest and instead learnt of the tragedy in a message from one of Johnwil’s friends.
Details
Marisha Isaacs: Die tyd toe ek die boodskap kry, ek was alleen by die huis, (The moment I received that, I was still alone at home.) Ek het nie eers geweet hoe om te voel nie. (I din’t even know how to feel.) Ek net gedink en gevra Here help my nou net dat ek…(I just thought and asked, “Lord, just help me now.) Is dit nou reg wat ek gelees het, (Is what I am reading correct?) toe voel dit vir my my bors wil toeslat. (It felt as if my chest wanted to collapse.)
V/O21: In a Statement, Sea Harvest says all the next of kin were contacted in the early hours of Saturday morning, and regularly updated on the search and rescue operation. The company confirmed that a representative of the Isaacs’ family, as well as Johnwill’s partner, were informed at their premises that he was among the 11 lost at sea.
Text on screen: “The company contacted the next-of-kin for all the vessel crew in the early hours of Saturday morning once we were able to confirm who had been rescued and who was missing. Thereafter, all the next-of-kin for the 11 crewmen were given updates during the search and rescue operation, including when it ceased. Company representatives visited all the families of the 11 men in person on Sunday, 19 May, to notify them that the MRCC had terminated the rescue operation. Details of the incident and the fact that Mr Isaacs was amongst the missing crewmen, as well as confirmation of the termination of the rescue effort, were communicated by the company in person to a family representative known to the company as Lizzy, and Mr Isaac’s partner, at the company’s premises where they were awaiting news of Mr Isaacs on Saturday and Sunday, 18 and 19 May, respectively.”
V/O22 By Saturday, there was still no sign of life… not even a lifejacket… just a few pieces of debris.
Erin Bates: How many days did the search continue for the Lepanto?
Dr Cleeve Robertson: So about two days, 48 hours, so that’s quite a long time.

V/O23 Finding the bodies would be almost impossible.

Dr Cleeve Robertson: The depth of the water out there is probably 300 meters or more and the commercial divers cannot operate at that depth. It would require very specialised equipment, remotely operated vehicles, a huge dive support vessel costing millions of dollars every day.
V/O24 On the Sunday, Sea Harvest informed the families that the Maritime Rescue Co-ordination Centre had called off the search and that the eleven crewmen were now presumed dead. Marisha struggled to understand why.
Marisha Isaacs: En soos ons ons vrae gevra het wat die rede was hoekom hulle so gou gestop het (When we asked them why they stopped the search so soon,)is dat hulle nie die nodige resources gehad het om aan te gaan nie. (we were told they did not have the necessary resources to continue.)
Erin Bates: Het julle enige vrae vir die maatskappy? (Do you have any questions for the company?)
Marisha Isaacs: Al wat ons wil weet is wat het rerig gebeur het en hoekom? (All we want to know is what really happened and why?)
V/O25 At a ceremony held at the docks a few days after the Lepanto went down, Sea Harvest encountered families anxious for closure. Benjamin van Wyk, whose son Jeremiah was among those lost at sea, wanted to know when the bodies would be brought to shore.
Cellphone video clip at sermon
Benjamin van Wyk: Ek wil gemoedsrus he in my hart dat ek kan weet dit is die liggaam van my seun. (I only want to be at peace, knowing how long it will take to bring back my son.) Hoe lank gaan dit vat? (How long will it take?)
V/O26 Jeremiah was 48 and had worked as a deckhand on the Lepanto for many years.
Erin Bates: Hoe is dit vir n pa om hier te sit onder daai closure? (What’s it like, as a father, to sit here without that closure?)
Benjamin van Wyk: Ons wil ten minste hom gaan begrawe (We, at least, want to give him a dignified burial) n waardige begrafnis gee en elke tyd blommetjies gaan opsit. (and place flowers on his grave.)
LINK: With the families of the deceased left with so many unanswered questions we asked Sea Harvest for an interview. They agreed but then they had a change of heart saying the tragedy was now the subject of an investigation.
V/O27 That investigation is being conducted by the SA Maritime Safety Authority which the company says is the appropriate forum to examine the facts around the incident.
In a written response, Sea Harvest says:
We take note of the speculation around the cause of the incident and certain unsubstantiated allegations made against the company. It says all its vessels are governed by a comprehensive and robust maintenance and servicing system as prescribed by the authorities.
It concludes by saying we are focused on ensuring the families of the missing crew are supported during this challenging time.
LINK: SAMSA is trawling for answers about the Lepanto, meanwhile families of 11 men are without bodies, without answers and without much hope.
V/O28 While SAMSA attempts to establish the facts around the sinking, a police investigation is also underway into the unnatural deaths of the 11 crew. It means the survivors will have to relive those final, chaotic moments as their colleagues cried for help before disappearing beneath the waves.

V/O Disaster strikes as a deep sea fishing trawler disappears off the coast of Cape Town.
UP SOUND: Nomrico Prins: Daar was nie eens kans om lifejackets nie, (There wasn’t even a chance to put on lifejackets…) als was so gou, seker 5 minute. (everything happened so quickly…) Toe’s als oor. (Five minutes, then it was all over.)
V/O We trace the final days of the MFV Lepanto, that took 11 men with it to its watery grave…
_________________________________________________________________________________________________
PROMO TWO: 21 seconds

VO: On a clear day off the coast of Cape Town, the unthinkable unfolds…
UP SOUND: Nomrico Prins: Op die een oomblik was ek nog op die skip (One moment I was on the vessel,) en die ander oomblik toe le ek in die water en spartel vir my lewe. (and the next moment I was fighting for my life.)

VO: A deep-sea fishing trawler sinks within minutes – leaving several crew members dead.

UPSOUND:. Nomrico Prins: En toe is dit als doodstil. (Then everything was dead quiet.)

PROMO 3:
VO: A deep-sea fishing trawler sinks within minutes, taking eleven crew members down with it.
UPSOUND:Nomrico Prins: Als was so gou, seker 5 minute. (It was all so quick) Toe’s als oor. Vyf minute toe’s als oor. (Five minutes, then it was all over.)
VO: Despite days of searching, none of their remains are recovered.
UPSOUND:Marisha Isaacs: Al wat ons wil weet is wat het rerig gebeur het en hoekom? (All we want to know is what really happened and why?)
VO: Now, their families are pleading for answers.

LINK: Erin Bates: In May, 11 men went down with the deep sea fishing trawler Lepanto off the cape coast. Nine men survived.
UPSOUND: Nomrico Prins: Want ek kon nog gehoor het hier onder hoe skree die mense (I could hear the cries below of the people: “Here mammie help, Here help”.(Lord mommy help, Lord help” 10;49.44 Agterna toe is dit als net doodstil. (Then there was dead silence)

They have not been told how long the investigation will take to establish the cause of the accident; if they will ever find the bodies and when they will find peace of mind to bury their loved ones. We will also get a first hand account from one of the survivors, Nomrico Prins, who told us they experienced engine problems on the Lepanto and had to return to port after only two days at sea. He will also share his story of what happened during those last hours and minutes before Lepanto disappeared. The company Sea Harvest declined to be interviewed at the last moment as they said an investigation by the South African Maritime Safety Authority (SAMSA) into the incident is still underway. In a Right of Reply they confirmed that Sea Harvest vessels are governed by a comprehensive maintenance system, with adherence to a robust and ongoing mandatory service regime as described by the authorities. They also said their efforts are focussed on ensuring the families of the missing crew are supported during this challenging time. We will ‘revisit’ the rescue mission going back hours and days when it happened through the story of one of the survivors, Nomrico Prins. For the bereaved families it is particularly difficult as they are waiting for the investigation to be concluded to find out why the accident happened. They are also waiting to hear when the men will officially be declared dead in order to bury their loved ones. Interviews: Two families who have lost a loved one: The Isaac family who lost Johnwill Isaacs, and Benjamin van Wyk who lost his son, Jeremiah. We will also hear from Cleeve Robertson, CEO NSRI what the search and rescue operation for the Lepanto crew entailed. _________________________________________________________________________________________________ Case Study: Benjamin van Wyk Marisha Isaacs Lena Isaacs Chrizelda Bock Cleeve Robertson Nomrico Prins Locations: Cape Town Other Footage Sources: South African Deep Sea Trawling Industry Association (SADSTIA): deep sea fishing trawler NSRI footage; TikTok clip of Armana rescuing the survivors; Cellphone clip taken by a survivor of the Lepanto on the slipway; Visuals from NSRI of the search and rescue mission Hidden Camera: No Legal: Yes Reason for legal: Legal is required as the families are making certain allegations against the company, Sea Harvest to which we received a ROR. June 2024 TX Date: 0000-00-00 Script: Script: Lost at Sea Duration: 12 minutes Up sound: Mayday mayday… V/O1 It’s exactly 26 minutes to four in the afternoon on Friday the 17th of May this year. A deep-sea vessel called MFV Armana issues a Mayday call. Another boat, the MFV Lepanto, is sinking off the Cape coast. Nomrico Prins: Op die een oomblik was ek nog op die skip (One moment I was on the vessel,) en die ander oomblik toe le ek in die water en spartel vir my lewe. (and the next moment I was fighting for my life.) Als het so gou gebeur. (Everything happened so quickly.) V/O2 Nomrico Prins is one of 20 crew on board the Lepanto, a fishing trawler owned by the company, Sea Harvest. He’s one of just nine survivors who jumped overboard and clung to a life raft. Nomrico Prins: Daar was nie eens kans om lifejackets nie, (There wasn’t even a chance to put on lifejackets…) als was so gou, seker 5 minute. (everything happened so quickly…) Toe’s als oor. (Five minutes, then it was all over.) V/O3 The remaining eleven crew, trapped inside the vessel, are heard crying for help as it disappears below the surface. V/O4: Now the subject of an investigation, the Lepanto tragedy has left nearly a dozen families grieving for loved ones lost at sea; their hopes for closure frustrated by uncertainty over whether their bodies will ever be retrieved. Pause music up LINK: Crews on deep sea trawlers spend days, weeks at sea, braving the elements. It's a hard job risking life and limb and safe return is never guaranteed. V/O5 Nomrico worked for Sea Harvest as a deckhand on the Lepanto for eleven years, forming a deep connection with his fellow crew. Nomrico Prins: Ek kan dit nie beskryf nie maar ons was soos n familie, elke dag saam. (I can’t describe it, but like a family, we were together every day.) Met elke trip is die 20 saam mekaar. (We were together every day…on every trip us 20 men were together) V/O6 Johnwill Isaacs left his home on the West Coast and signed up for the fishing life at just 17. Lena Isaacs: Johnwill’s mother - En hy het vir my gese hy wil nou beginne werk, hy wil nou see toe gaan. (Then he told me he wants to work - he wants to work at sea) Toe het ek altyd teen die skare geskop en vir hom gese my hart is nie vir jou om op die see te werk nie (I kicked against the idea and said to him, “My heart doesn’t want you to go to sea”.) Maar ek het vir die Here gevra en die Here het my kalmte gegee dat hy maar gegaan het.(But then I asked the Lord, and He brought me peace - so I let my son go.) V/O7 Johnwill, who had a close relationship with his two sisters, worked as deckhand on the Lepanto for 5 years. Marisha Isaacs: Johnwill’s sister - As hy so van die see afgekom het (When he returned from the sea,) sal hy altyd unexpected opdaag by my, net om te kom hello se. (he would drop by unexpectedly, just to say hello,) Chrizelda Bock: Johnwill’s sister: Hy was baie lief vir diere.(He was fond of animals.) Vriendelike man. (A friendly man.) V/O8 The last time Johnwill’s family saw him alive was when he left for Cape Town’s harbour on the Tuesday before the tragedy. Fade to black V/9 The Lepanto left Cape Town port at 10 to 10 on 14th of May with 20 crew on board including Johnwill and Nomrico. According to Nomrico the vessel soon experienced engine trouble and had to return to port barely 24 hours later. Nomrico Prins: Daar n problem op die main enjin soos hulle gese het (They said there was a problem with the main engine…) Dit was die fuel timing van die skip.(the fuel timing of the vessel was out.) Up sound V/O10 This video is taken from the deck of the Lepanto while it was being maintained in Cape Town harbour. V/O11 After 14 hours on the slipway, the Lepanto returned to sea at 8 minutes past 4 on that Thursday afternoon. Nomrico Prins: Ons het die donderdag aand, daai is omtrent nege uur (On the Thursday night, ‘round about nine o’clock,) wat die kaptein vir ons gese het ons gaan nou weer skiet (the captain said we are going to shoot again) om te kyk of als reg is (to see if everything is alright -)of die enjin die krag het om te tou.(if the engine still has power to hoist.) V/O12 Shooting refers to sending the fishing gear to the seabed. Pause V/O13 At 2pm on Friday the 17th of May, the captain ordered that the trawl doors be shut. Minutes later disaster struck. Nomrico Prins: Ons, ek was seker nog nie af by die trappies om te kom by die port side (I barely reached the bottom of the steps) en toe sien ek net hier gaan le die skip (when I saw the ship tilting…) en ek se vir myself “kom nou kom nou kom nou” (I said to myself, “Come now, come now!”) ek se nog vir myself “kom nou kom nou” (I said to myself, “Come now, come now!”) en ek het net gevoel een gryp my van agter af en hy ruk my toe op. (Then I felt someone grab me from behind and he pulled me up.) En hy se Rico die skip gaat val (And he said, “Rico the vessel is going to fall!”) en toe het hy al klaar gesien die mast touch die water (And then he already saw the mast falling into the water,) en ‘doef’ toe le die skip op sy een kant. (and ‘“dooof”! The ship was lying on its side.) V/O14 Nomrico’s recollection of those last, chaotic minutes is sketchy. He was overcome with shock but he says he heard nothing out of the ordinary in the minutes before the ship went down. At least one of the crew could not swim Nomrico Prins: En hy het net gese ouens is alright ek kan nie swem nie (And he said, “No, guys. It’s alright. I can’t swim.) en toe gaan hy af die eerste keer (Then he lifted his hands like this and went down the first time.) Toe kom hy weer op. (Then he came up again, then went straight down.) Toe gat hy net straight af en ons het hom nooit weer gesien nie.(We never saw him after that.) LONG PAUSE here Nomrico Prins: Want ek kon net gehoor het hoe daai drie keer geskree het (All I could hear were the screams.) Here mammie, help Here. En toe is dit als doodstil.(God, mommy, help God”,) Toe’s als doodstil. (and then it was dead quiet.) Toe is daar niks meer geskreery nie.(There was no more crying.) LONG PAUSE V/O15 One would think being able to swim is key to surviving an accident at sea. But the internationally recognised certifications standard required by all seafarers working on commercial vessels only teaches basic survival techniques, not how to swim. Pause V/O16 The nine survivors were rescued by the Armana, the vessel that had issued the original Mayday. UP cellphone video clip of the rescue V/O17 Four other vessels responded to a mayday broadcast by the Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre, and the National Sea Rescue Institute was alerted. LINK: One of the NSRI rescue craft left from this space at Hout Bay harbour and headed to the Lepanto’s last known location, 35 nautical miles from the coast. Dr Cleeve Robertson - CEO National Sea Rescue Institute: When the crew got on scene, understanding they arrived fairly close to last light and then searched into the night. V/O18 Dr Cleeve Robertsona heads up the NSRI, staffed by dedicated volunteers. Dr Cleeve Robertson: To assist them search at night they used illumination flares, very much like a distress signal in the darkness of night, it is very difficult. V/O19 The NRSI saves hundreds of fishers in distress every year. On this mission their crew battled the darkness, howling 40 knot winds and 4 to 6 meter swells. Pause V/O20 Most of the next of kin were notified of the incident that same evening. Marisha says her family never received a call from Sea Harvest and instead learnt of the tragedy in a message from one of Johnwil’s friends. Details Marisha Isaacs: Die tyd toe ek die boodskap kry, ek was alleen by die huis, (The moment I received that, I was still alone at home.) Ek het nie eers geweet hoe om te voel nie. (I din’t even know how to feel.) Ek net gedink en gevra Here help my nou net dat ek…(I just thought and asked, “Lord, just help me now.) Is dit nou reg wat ek gelees het, (Is what I am reading correct?) toe voel dit vir my my bors wil toeslat. (It felt as if my chest wanted to collapse.) V/O21: In a Statement, Sea Harvest says all the next of kin were contacted in the early hours of Saturday morning, and regularly updated on the search and rescue operation. The company confirmed that a representative of the Isaacs’ family, as well as Johnwill’s partner, were informed at their premises that he was among the 11 lost at sea. Text on screen: “The company contacted the next-of-kin for all the vessel crew in the early hours of Saturday morning once we were able to confirm who had been rescued and who was missing. Thereafter, all the next-of-kin for the 11 crewmen were given updates during the search and rescue operation, including when it ceased. Company representatives visited all the families of the 11 men in person on Sunday, 19 May, to notify them that the MRCC had terminated the rescue operation. Details of the incident and the fact that Mr Isaacs was amongst the missing crewmen, as well as confirmation of the termination of the rescue effort, were communicated by the company in person to a family representative known to the company as Lizzy, and Mr Isaac’s partner, at the company’s premises where they were awaiting news of Mr Isaacs on Saturday and Sunday, 18 and 19 May, respectively.” V/O22 By Saturday, there was still no sign of life… not even a lifejacket… just a few pieces of debris. Erin Bates: How many days did the search continue for the Lepanto? Dr Cleeve Robertson: So about two days, 48 hours, so that’s quite a long time. V/O23 Finding the bodies would be almost impossible. Dr Cleeve Robertson: The depth of the water out there is probably 300 meters or more and the commercial divers cannot operate at that depth. It would require very specialised equipment, remotely operated vehicles, a huge dive support vessel costing millions of dollars every day. V/O24 On the Sunday, Sea Harvest informed the families that the Maritime Rescue Co-ordination Centre had called off the search and that the eleven crewmen were now presumed dead. Marisha struggled to understand why. Marisha Isaacs: En soos ons ons vrae gevra het wat die rede was hoekom hulle so gou gestop het (When we asked them why they stopped the search so soon,)is dat hulle nie die nodige resources gehad het om aan te gaan nie. (we were told they did not have the necessary resources to continue.) Erin Bates: Het julle enige vrae vir die maatskappy? (Do you have any questions for the company?) Marisha Isaacs: Al wat ons wil weet is wat het rerig gebeur het en hoekom? (All we want to know is what really happened and why?) V/O25 At a ceremony held at the docks a few days after the Lepanto went down, Sea Harvest encountered families anxious for closure. Benjamin van Wyk, whose son Jeremiah was among those lost at sea, wanted to know when the bodies would be brought to shore. Cellphone video clip at sermon Benjamin van Wyk: Ek wil gemoedsrus he in my hart dat ek kan weet dit is die liggaam van my seun. (I only want to be at peace, knowing how long it will take to bring back my son.) Hoe lank gaan dit vat? (How long will it take?) V/O26 Jeremiah was 48 and had worked as a deckhand on the Lepanto for many years. Erin Bates: Hoe is dit vir n pa om hier te sit onder daai closure? (What’s it like, as a father, to sit here without that closure?) Benjamin van Wyk: Ons wil ten minste hom gaan begrawe (We, at least, want to give him a dignified burial) n waardige begrafnis gee en elke tyd blommetjies gaan opsit. (and place flowers on his grave.) LINK: With the families of the deceased left with so many unanswered questions we asked Sea Harvest for an interview. They agreed but then they had a change of heart saying the tragedy was now the subject of an investigation. V/O27 That investigation is being conducted by the SA Maritime Safety Authority which the company says is the appropriate forum to examine the facts around the incident. In a written response, Sea Harvest says: We take note of the speculation around the cause of the incident and certain unsubstantiated allegations made against the company. It says all its vessels are governed by a comprehensive and robust maintenance and servicing system as prescribed by the authorities. It concludes by saying we are focused on ensuring the families of the missing crew are supported during this challenging time. LINK: SAMSA is trawling for answers about the Lepanto, meanwhile families of 11 men are without bodies, without answers and without much hope. V/O28 While SAMSA attempts to establish the facts around the sinking, a police investigation is also underway into the unnatural deaths of the 11 crew. It means the survivors will have to relive those final, chaotic moments as their colleagues cried for help before disappearing beneath the waves. __________________________________________________________________________________________________ PROMO ONE: 21 seconds V/O Disaster strikes as a deep sea fishing trawler disappears off the coast of Cape Town. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): When a deep sea fishing trawler sank off the coast of Cape Town, only 9 men survived, 11 went missing. Now their families are asking what happened and why.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: On Friday 17 May the unexplainable and most unexpected happened: The Lepanto, a deep sea fishing trawler, disappeared in a matter of minutes off the coast of Table Bay. Two life rafts were on board. Nine men clung onto the one, the second blew away in the wind. Eleven men could not be saved and disappeared into the ocean.
metadata.Summary: On Thursday 16 May the MFV Lepanto deep sea fishing trawler were brought back due to some enjin problems. Later that day, the Lepanto carrying 20 crew members went back out to sea to continue their fishing. They were trawling hake 34 nautical miles west off Slangkop light. On Friday 17 May at 15h30 a distress call came from the MFV Armana, a vessel trawling fish near the Lepanto. The Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre picked up the Mayday call from the Armanis that the Lepanto was in trouble and sinking rapidly. Within 3 minutes the vessel vanished. The only sign of life were 9 crew hanging onto a life raft desperate to get to the Armanis as they contend with meter swells and rough seas. They were not wearing any life jackets but with the assistance of the men on the Armanis they were brought safely onto the vessel. The NSRI were called in to assist and sent a rescue craft to the site where the Lepanto disappeared. They had to race to the site which was 35 nautical miles away and took an hour. Three more vessels joined the search but there was no sign of life, life jackets or the usual signs like oil spills and debris. The search and rescue continued on Saturday but even with the help of a fixed wing aircraft to scan the ocean, they could not find any signs of life, only a few pieces of debris floating in the area where the Lepanto disappeared. The depth of the ocean was measured at 300 meters, too deep to send divers down to look for the bodies. It is presumed that the Lepanto turned upside down, trapping the men underneath. On Sunday, barely three days later, the search was called off. The decision was made by The Maritime Rescue Operation Centre. Sea Harvest employer, CEO Felix Rhateb stated: “in view of the significant time elapsed since the accident we are calling off the search. Tragically, the men are now presumed drowned.” It is reportedly one of the worst maritime fishing accidents in the history of Sea Harvest, said Rhateb when he met with the families. Also present at a gathering on Tuesday with the families were the mayor of Cape Town, the premier, and the minister of DEFF to give condolences. At a special service held for the families on Thursday at the Cruise Terminal in Cape Town both survivors and family members spoke out. Benjamin van Wyk lost his son Jeremiah. He was asking where the bodies are? Why did they not go down looking for the men? And how can he find peace if there is no corpse to bury. A moment of silence was given for the missing men presumed drowned. One by one the names of the eleven men were called out. In the Isaacs home near Chatsworth on the West Coast, there is so much grief among the sisters and the mother. They lost their 26 year old brother, Johnwill, nicknamed “Jangle”. They too have questions about the accident and what could have happened why they have lost the center of the family so early in his life.
metadata.Further information: A tragedy of this magnitude runs deep in the circles of seafaring men when they rely on each other through storms and difficulties. The families who lost sons and husbands are blaming Sea Harvest for giving up and not spending money to find the bodies at the bottom of the sea and bringing them back to shore to be buried. An investigation has been launched by the South African Maritime Safety Authority (SAMSA) into the history of the vessel, the repairs conducted and the service record amongst others. The investigation is ongoing and we will not be able to interview SAMSA at this stage.
